speaker: Dylan Patel
title: Dylan Patel — The single biggest bottleneck to scaling AI compute
question: In AI hardware, why can't you escape leading-edge chip shortages by designing modern accelerators on abundant older process nodes like 7nm?
guest: Even if you design a brand-new chip on seven nanometer optimized for modern numerics, the performance difference is still much larger than the raw FLOPs difference suggests. It's easy to boil things down to FLOPs per watt or FLOPs per dollar, but that's not a fair comparison because frontier models don't run on a single chip—they run split across hundreds of chips at a time. Every time you cross from one chip to another, there is an efficiency loss over high-speed electrical links, adding latency and power costs. You have a huge communication ladder: on-chip data moves at tens to hundreds of terabytes per second, between chips in a rack it's on the order of terabytes per second, and across racks it drops another order of magnitude to roughly a hundred gigabytes per second. Shrinking the process node packs far more compute into each fast communication domain. That's why real-world inference performance compounds across FLOPs per chip, memory bandwidth, and inter-chip networking—creating something like a 20x gap at target latency between Hopper and Blackwell rather than just a 2x or 3x FLOPs gap.

points.core: Frontier AI models must split execution across hundreds of chips rather than one.
points.note: Accept: multi-chip distributed serving or training where large models exceed a single chip and require frequent cross-chip communication. Do not credit: generic statements that AI models are large without tying them to multi-chip execution.

points.core: Data-transfer bandwidth drops roughly an order of magnitude at each physical hardware boundary.
points.note: Accept: communication hierarchy stepping down steeply from on-chip (tens/hundreds of TB/s) to intra-rack (~TB/s) to inter-rack (~100 GB/s), incurring latency and power penalties whenever crossing chip boundaries. Do not credit: vague mentions that networking matters without the multi-tier bandwidth drop.

points.core: Packing more compute per die avoids cross-chip penalties to multiply real-world serving throughput.
points.note: Accept: shrinking process nodes keeping more work inside faster on-chip/intra-rack domains so system-level inference performance compounds far beyond raw FLOPs ratios (e.g., 10-20x vs 2-3x). Do not credit: simply repeating that newer nodes are faster or more power-efficient per transistor.

models.label: Claude Fable 5.2
models.answer:
Because the wafer is only one of several bottlenecks, and moving to an older node doesn't relieve the others while making the chip itself much worse.

First, performance per watt is the binding constraint in AI data centers. A 7nm design has roughly a third to half the transistor density of 3nm-class nodes and markedly worse energy efficiency, so matching the same compute needs far more silicon, power, cooling, and rack space. Since power and data center capacity are themselves scarce, a less efficient chip is uncompetitive on total cost of ownership even if it's cheap to make.

Second, the scarce inputs are shared across nodes. Any modern accelerator still needs high-bandwidth memory (HBM) and advanced packaging such as TSMC's CoWoS, both of which are supply-constrained regardless of the logic node. Larger, less dense dies actually consume more packaging and interposer area per unit of compute.

Third, 7nm isn't truly abundant: it's still an EUV-era node concentrated at TSMC and Samsung, and capacity is limited.

Finally, redesigning for a different node takes years and substantial engineering cost.

points.why: The response discusses the resources needed to match compute but never says that frontier models must execute across many chips.
The response mentions high-bandwidth memory but gives no bandwidth hierarchy from on-chip to intra-rack to inter-rack communication.
The response links transistor density to power and cost but never explains how keeping more work on each die avoids communication penalties and multiplies serving throughput.

models.label: Gemini Carbon
models.answer: Building modern AI accelerators on older nodes like 7nm fails to solve shortages because the tightest supply bottlenecks lie outside the logic wafer itself, while older silicon breaks data center economics. First, AI hardware output is heavily constrained by High Bandwidth Memory (HBM) and advanced 2.5D packaging capacity like TSMC’s CoWoS, rather than leading-edge lithography alone. Moving compute logic to 7nm cannot bypass those shared bottlenecks—in fact, it worsens them. Flagship accelerators already push against the maximum photomask reticle size limit on 3nm and 4nm. Because 7nm offers roughly half the transistor density, matching modern compute throughput and on-chip SRAM capacity requires splitting workloads across more dies and packages, consuming even more scarce CoWoS interposer area, HBM stacks, and high-speed networking. Finally, modern AI clusters are strictly power- and thermal-constrained. Older nodes burn significantly more energy per operation and across chip-to-chip interconnects, slashing compute performance per megawatt and inflating cooling, networking, and facility costs until the total cost of ownership becomes uncompetitive—even if the 7nm wafers themselves were cheap and plentiful.

points.why: The response ties splitting workloads across more dies to compensating for 7nm density, but never explains that frontier models exceed a single accelerator and require distributed execution.
The response mentions networking and interconnect power costs but omits the steep bandwidth drops from on-chip to intra-rack to inter-rack communication.
The response links lower density to more dies and higher interconnect costs but does not explain how keeping more work on-chip compounds serving throughput beyond the raw FLOPs gain.

models.label: Claude Opus 5.5
models.answer:
Older nodes don't solve the problem, because AI accelerators compete mainly on compute per watt and per square millimeter, and those come from transistor density. A die can't exceed the lithography reticle limit of roughly 800 mm², so a 7nm chip holds far fewer transistors than a 4nm or 3nm chip of the same size. Matching a leading-edge part would take more chips. That means more power, more cooling, more rack space, and more chip-to-chip communication, which adds latency and energy overhead. Data centers are increasingly limited by power, and electricity and facility costs make up most of the total cost of ownership. An inefficient chip that's cheap to buy can still be the more expensive one to run.

The shortage also isn't only about the logic node. The real chokepoints have often been high-bandwidth memory (HBM) and advanced packaging such as TSMC's CoWoS, and a 7nm design needs both just as much. Finally, 7nm capacity isn't especially plentiful at the scale AI demands. For companies cut off by export controls, like Huawei on SMIC's 7nm process, older-node chips are a fallback with poorer yields and efficiency, not an escape.

points.why: The response says more 7 nm chips would be needed to match a leading-edge part but never establishes that frontier models require distributed execution across many chips.
The response identifies latency and energy overhead from chip-to-chip communication but omits the steep bandwidth drops from on-chip to intra-rack to inter-rack communication.
The response links lower compute density to more cross-chip overhead but does not explain how higher compute density translates into serving throughput gains larger than the raw FLOPs gap.

models.label: Gemini Neon
models.answer:
Designing modern AI accelerators on older nodes like 7nm fails to bypass supply shortages primarily because leading-edge logic wafers are rarely the sole bottleneck. High-performance AI chips rely heavily on High Bandwidth Memory (HBM) and advanced 2.5D packaging, such as TSMC's CoWoS, to feed data to compute units. A 7nm accelerator still competes for the exact same scarce HBM stacks and packaging capacity as a 3nm or 4nm chip.

Even if packaging were abundant, older nodes hit severe physical and economic walls. Leading AI dies are already near the reticle limit—the maximum physical size a lithography scanner can print. Stepping back to 7nm slashes transistor density, leaving far less room for compute cores and on-chip SRAM per die. Matching the performance of a modern cluster therefore requires many more chips, which multiplies interconnect overhead, cooling demands, and energy consumption. Because older nodes deliver substantially worse performance per watt, they quickly become uncompetitive in power-constrained data centers, where electricity and infrastructure dominate total cost of ownership.

points.why: The response says older nodes need more chips to match cluster performance but does not say a single frontier model must run across many chips.
The response mentions interconnect overhead but gives no bandwidth hierarchy across on-chip, intra-rack, and inter-rack communication.
The response links lower compute density to more chips and greater interconnect overhead but does not explain how avoiding those transfers raises serving throughput beyond the raw FLOPs gain.

models.label: GPT-6.2-Sol
models.answer:
You can build capable AI accelerators on 7 nm. The hard part is matching the performance and operating cost of a leading-edge accelerator for the same workload.

An older node generally fits fewer transistors per square millimeter and uses more energy for the same computation. Matching a newer chip’s compute and on-chip memory can require a larger die, which yields fewer chips per wafer and is more likely to contain a manufacturing defect. If the design exceeds the maximum die size, you can split it across chiplets or use more accelerators, but moving data between them adds power, latency, and packaging or networking costs. In a power-limited data center, lower performance per watt also means less compute per rack.

Extra 7 nm wafer capacity only addresses the logic supply. High-bandwidth memory and advanced packaging can be bottlenecks in their own right. Older nodes can ease shortages for workloads that fit their performance and power budgets, while replacing top-end accelerators at scale can shift the bottleneck elsewhere.

points.why: The response presents multi-accelerator execution as a workaround for die-size limits and does not explain why frontier models themselves require distributed execution.
The response mentions cross-chip power and latency costs but omits the steep bandwidth drops from on-chip to intra-rack to inter-rack communication.
The response identifies the cost of splitting a design but does not explain how keeping more work on each die multiplies serving throughput beyond the raw FLOPs gain.

models.label: GPT-6.2-Astra
models.answer:
You can build an AI accelerator on 7nm. The hard part is matching a leading-edge chip’s throughput within the same power and space limits. On 7nm, the same compute logic generally takes up more silicon and uses more energy per operation. A larger die means fewer dies per wafer and a greater chance that a defect spoils one. There’s also a limit to how large a die can be.

You can split the work across more chips, but moving data between them costs energy and can slow the workload. The resulting system may need more boards, power, and cooling. It may also depend on the same scarce high-bandwidth memory and advanced packaging as a leading-edge design.

Older nodes can make sense when lower performance is acceptable or power and space are plentiful. Abundant 7nm wafer capacity alone doesn’t guarantee abundant AI compute at a competitive cost.

points.why: The response presents using more chips as an option without explaining that frontier models exceed a single chip’s capacity and require distributed execution.
The response mentions cross-chip energy and slowdown but omits the steep bandwidth drops from on-chip to intra-rack to inter-rack communication.
The response identifies cross-chip overhead without explaining how denser dies keep more work on-chip and compound serving throughput beyond the raw FLOPs advantage.
